# Automated Storage and Retrieval System: Multi-Level Rack Configuration with Variable Vertical Pitch

## System Overview

The automated storage and retrieval system disclosed herein comprises a storage array configured with a plurality of storage spaces arranged on racks positioned along picking aisles. These aisles extend across multiple level decks, forming a structured framework that supports efficient item storage and retrieval operations throughout the facility.

## Deck and Aisle Configuration

Each aisle within the storage array is configured to communicate with at least one deck, establishing the necessary connectivity between the storage levels and the transport infrastructure. The decks and aisles work in concert to create a continuous rolling surface at every deck level, upon which an autonomous transport vehicle can traverse. This rolling surface configuration ensures that the transport vehicle maintains consistent, unobstructed movement across each level of the storage array, facilitating seamless navigation throughout the system.

## Multi-Level Rack Accessibility

A distinguishing feature of this system is the arrangement of racks along at least one aisle at each deck level. Rather than confining storage to a single elevation, these racks are positioned at multiple distinct rack levels within that aisle. Critically, all of these multiple rack levels remain accessible from a single, common rolling surface. This design eliminates the need for the transport vehicle to transition between separate physical decks or platforms to access different storage heights within the same aisle, as the vehicle can reach multiple rack levels directly from its position on the shared rolling surface.

## Variable Vertical Pitch Architecture

The vertical pitch—defined as the spacing distance between successive rack levels—is not uniform throughout a given aisle. Instead, this vertical pitch varies across different portions or sections of the aisle. This variable pitch architecture provides significant flexibility in configuring the storage spaces, allowing the system to accommodate items of differing dimensions, optimize storage density, or address other operational requirements that may differ from one section of the aisle to another.

## Coordinated Pitch for Sequential Multi-Pick Operations

Despite the variation in vertical pitch across different aisle portions, this spacing is deliberately coordinated between the various sections. This coordination is not incidental but is purposefully engineered to enable the autonomous transport vehicle to execute multiple picking operations in a defined, ordered sequence during a single pass through the aisle. By synchronizing the vertical pitch relationships between different aisle portions, the system allows the transport vehicle to efficiently access multiple storage locations at varying rack levels without requiring multiple separate passes through the aisle. This coordinated approach significantly enhances retrieval efficiency, as the vehicle can complete several ordered picks in one continuous trip, thereby reducing overall cycle time and improving the throughput of the automated storage and retrieval system.

## Operational Benefits

This configuration—combining a common rolling surface with multiple accessible rack levels and a strategically coordinated variable vertical pitch—represents a substantial advancement in automated storage system design. It allows for greater flexibility in storage space utilization while simultaneously enabling more efficient transport vehicle operations, as a single vehicle pass can accomplish what might otherwise require multiple separate retrieval trips in conventional systems with uniform, uncoordinated rack spacing.

# Optimizing Multi-Level Rack Configurations for Automated Storage and Retrieval Systems

## Background and Problem Statement

Automated storage and retrieval systems (AS/RS) have become foundational infrastructure in modern warehousing and distribution operations, where the efficient use of vertical and horizontal space directly impacts operational costs and throughput capacity. Traditional AS/RS designs typically employ a fixed vertical pitch between rack levels—meaning the spacing between consecutive shelves or storage levels remains constant throughout the entire rack structure. While this uniformity simplifies mechanical design and vehicle control logic, it imposes significant limitations on both storage density and retrieval efficiency.

The core challenge addressed by this work is twofold. First, conventional fixed-pitch systems fail to account for the natural variation in item sizes that occurs across different rack levels or storage zones, often forcing operators to either waste vertical space by accommodating the tallest expected item at every level, or to constrain inventory placement in ways that reduce flexibility. Second, and perhaps more critically, fixed-pitch configurations constrain how autonomous transport vehicles can interact with the rack structure. In many conventional systems, a vehicle must complete a full pick-and-return cycle—traveling to a single storage location, retrieving an item, and returning to a transfer point—before it can proceed to the next pick location, even when multiple required items are located along the same aisle.

## Proposed Solution: Variable Vertical Pitch Rack Configuration

To address these limitations, the proposed system introduces a multi-level rack configuration in which the vertical pitch—the distance between consecutive rack levels—is deliberately varied along the height of the storage structure within a given picking aisle. Rather than treating vertical spacing as a fixed mechanical constraint, this variable pitch design allows the rack architecture to be tailored to specific storage and retrieval requirements, whether that means accommodating heterogeneous item dimensions, optimizing space utilization for high-density storage zones, or creating structural configurations that facilitate more efficient vehicle movement patterns.

A critical enabling feature of this configuration is that it maintains **common rolling surfaces** that span multiple rack levels within the aisle. This means that autonomous transport vehicles are not confined to a single level or forced to disengage from one level before accessing another; instead, the vehicles can traverse a shared surface that provides access to multiple storage levels as needed. This structural continuity is what makes advanced multi-pick operations possible, since the vehicle's chassis and lift mechanisms can interact with several rack levels without requiring a return to a home position or transfer station between each interaction.

## Enabling Multi-Item Retrieval in a Single Pass

The most significant operational advantage of this variable-pitch, common-rolling-surface design is that it enables an autonomous transport vehicle to execute **multiple item picks in an ordered sequence during a single pass through the aisle**. Rather than the vehicle entering the aisle, retrieving one item, exiting, and re-entering to retrieve a second item—a process that incurs substantial time overhead due to repeated acceleration, deceleration, and positioning maneuvers—the vehicle can instead traverse the aisle once, picking up multiple items from different rack levels and different horizontal positions in a coordinated, sequential manner.

This capability fundamentally changes the throughput calculus of the retrieval system. Order fulfillment operations, which frequently require the collection of multiple distinct items to complete a customer order or batch shipment, can be executed far more efficiently when a single vehicle pass can satisfy several pick requirements simultaneously. The vehicle's control system determines the optimal sequence of picks based on the physical layout of the variable-pitch rack levels, the location of required items, and the vehicle's movement capabilities, allowing it to plan a path that minimizes redundant travel while maximizing the number of successful retrievals per aisle traversal.

## Advantages Over Conventional Fixed-Pitch Systems

When compared to traditional fixed-pitch storage architectures, this variable vertical pitch approach offers several compounding benefits:

1. **Improved Storage Density**: By tailoring vertical spacing to actual item dimensions and storage requirements at each level, the system reduces wasted vertical space that would otherwise result from uniform, worst-case spacing assumptions.

2. **Reduced Vehicle Travel Time**: Since vehicles can complete multiple picks without exiting and re-entering the aisle, the cumulative travel distance and time required to fulfill multi-item orders is substantially reduced.

3. **Increased Retrieval Throughput**: The ability to batch multiple picks into a single aisle pass directly translates into a higher volume of completed retrievals per unit of time, improving the overall capacity of the automated system.

4. **Enhanced Operational Flexibility**: The common rolling surface architecture allows the system to adapt to varying inventory profiles and order patterns without requiring reconfiguration of the underlying rack structure for each change in item mix.

5. **Better Resource Utilization**: Because fewer vehicle trips are needed to accomplish the same retrieval workload, the system can either operate with fewer vehicles for a given throughput target or achieve higher throughput with the same fleet size, improving capital efficiency.

## Conclusion

This approach to rack design represents a meaningful departure from conventional AS/RS architecture by treating vertical pitch as a configurable design parameter rather than a fixed constraint, while simultaneously enabling autonomous vehicles to leverage common rolling surfaces for efficient multi-level access. The resulting capability for ordered, multi-item picking within a single aisle pass addresses core inefficiencies present in traditional systems, offering a pathway to significantly improved storage density and retrieval throughput in automated warehousing environments.

# Understanding Storage Arrays: The Backbone of Modern Data Management

A storage array is a specialized hardware system designed to store, manage, and provide access to large volumes of digital data. Unlike a single hard drive or storage device, a storage array combines multiple disks—whether hard disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), or a hybrid of both—into a unified system that offers greater capacity, reliability, and performance than any individual component could provide alone.

## How Storage Arrays Work

At its core, a storage array uses a controller to manage the flow of data between connected servers and the physical storage media. This controller handles critical functions such as data distribution, redundancy, and performance optimization. Most storage arrays implement RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) configurations, which allow data to be spread across multiple disks in ways that either improve speed, ensure fault tolerance, or both. If one disk fails, RAID technology often allows the array to continue operating without data loss, while a replacement drive is installed.

## Types of Storage Arrays

There are several categories of storage arrays, each suited to different needs:

- **Direct-Attached Storage (DAS)**: Connected directly to a single server, offering simplicity and speed for smaller-scale operations.
- **Network-Attached Storage (NAS)**: Connected to a network, allowing multiple users and devices to access shared storage simultaneously.
- **Storage Area Networks (SAN)**: A more complex, high-performance solution that provides block-level storage accessible by multiple servers, commonly used in enterprise environments.

## Why Storage Arrays Matter

Organizations rely on storage arrays for several key reasons:

**Scalability** – As data needs grow, additional drives or array units can often be added without disrupting existing operations.

**Redundancy and Reliability** – Built-in fault tolerance mechanisms protect against data loss due to hardware failure, which is critical for businesses that cannot afford downtime.

**Performance** – By distributing data across multiple disks, arrays can achieve faster read and write speeds than single-disk systems, which is essential for applications like databases, virtualization, and high-transaction environments.

**Centralized Management** – Storage arrays consolidate data storage, making it easier for IT teams to monitor, back up, and secure information from a single point of control.

## Storage Arrays in the Modern Landscape

As businesses increasingly move toward cloud computing and hybrid infrastructures, storage arrays continue to evolve. Modern arrays often integrate with cloud services, offering tiered storage solutions that balance cost and performance. Flash-based storage arrays, in particular, have become popular for their speed advantages over traditional spinning disks, especially in environments where rapid data access is critical, such as financial services, healthcare, and real-time analytics.

## Conclusion

Storage arrays represent a fundamental building block of modern IT infrastructure. By combining multiple storage devices into a cohesive, manageable system, they provide the capacity, speed, and resilience that organizations need to handle ever-growing volumes of data. Whether supporting a small business network or powering a global enterprise, storage arrays remain essential to ensuring that data remains accessible, secure, and readily available when needed.

# Warehouse Storage Array: Multi-Level Deck System with Variable Rack Pitch

## System Overview

The storage array consists of parallel picking aisles flanked by multi-level rack decks, serviced by autonomous transport vehicles (ATVs) operating on guided or free-navigation paths. The core innovation addressed here is **variable rack pitch**—the deliberate variation in horizontal spacing between storage bays—which enables ATVs to execute multiple picks per aisle traversal rather than requiring a dedicated stop-and-return cycle for each SKU.

---

## 1. Structural Configuration

### 1.1 Aisle Geometry
- **Aisle width**: Sized to ATV footprint plus clearance tolerances (typically 1.2–1.8m for narrow-aisle systems)
- **Deck levels**: 3–7 vertical tiers per rack face, accessed via lift mechanisms integrated into the ATV chassis or via fixed-level shuttle handoff
- **Rack pitch**: The center-to-center distance between adjacent storage bays along the aisle's longitudinal axis

### 1.2 Rack Pitch Variability
Rather than uniform bay spacing, pitch is stratified according to:

| Zone | Pitch Range | SKU Velocity Class | Rationale |
|------|------------|--------------------|-----------|
| High-density | 300–450mm | Fast-movers (A-class) | Tight spacing maximizes pick density per meter of travel |
| Standard | 500–750mm | Medium-movers (B-class) | Balances accessibility with storage efficiency |
| Extended | 800–1200mm | Slow-movers/bulk (C-class) | Accommodates larger totes, pallets, or irregular dimensions |

---

## 2. Mechanics of Multi-Pick Aisle Passes

### 2.1 The Core Principle
An ATV traversing an aisle must decelerate, stop, extend/retract a pick mechanism (shuttle arm, robotic gripper, or conveyor interface), and re-accelerate for each discrete pick location. Where rack pitch is **tight and uniform across a pick cluster**, the ATV can:

- Maintain a **near-continuous crawl speed** rather than full stop-start cycles
- Execute **sequential micro-stops** within a single motion envelope, since deceleration/acceleration distances overlap between adjacent bays
- Batch multiple pick confirmations into one control-loop pass, reducing communication overhead with the WMS

### 2.2 Pitch-to-Velocity Relationship
The achievable pick rate per aisle pass is governed by:

```
N_picks = L_aisle / (P_avg + D_stop)
```

Where:
- `L_aisle` = usable aisle length
- `P_avg` = average rack pitch in the active zone
- `D_stop` = incremental distance penalty per stop (dependent on ATV deceleration profile)

**Tighter pitch reduces the denominator's dominant term**, allowing more picks within fixed aisle length—but only if pitch remains below the ATV's minimum stop-recovery distance threshold, below which stops merge into a single continuous "creep" maneuver rather than discrete events.

### 2.3 Zone Transition Handling
When an ATV's pick list spans multiple pitch zones (e.g., a batch order pulling both A-class and C-class items), the routing algorithm must:

1. **Cluster picks by zone** to front-load tight-pitch (high-frequency stop) segments where momentum conservation is most beneficial
2. Insert **buffer acceleration segments** at zone boundaries to re-normalize speed before encountering wider-pitch bays
3. Avoid oscillating between zones mid-batch, which reintroduces full stop-start penalties and negates pitch-density gains

---

## 3. ATV Behavior Adaptation

### 3.1 Velocity Profiling
ATV firmware maintains distinct motion profiles per pitch zone:
- **Tight-pitch mode**: Low peak velocity, minimal deceleration depth, rapid pick-arm cycling synchronized to bay spacing
- **Standard-pitch mode**: Moderate velocity with full stop-pick-go cycles
- **Extended-pitch mode**: Higher peak velocity between stops, since longer inter-bay distance allows full acceleration recovery

### 3.2 Pick Sequencing Optimization
The warehouse control system (WCS) generates pick paths that:
- Prioritize **same-zone consolidation** within a single order batch
- Calculate whether pitch-driven speed gains offset the SKU-scatter penalty of non-optimal shelf assignment
- Dynamically reassign SKU slotting (slotting optimization) based on observed pick frequency, effectively *tuning the pitch zones to match demand patterns* over time

---

## 4. Trade-offs and Constraints

| Factor | Tight Pitch Benefit | Tight Pitch Cost |
|--------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Picks/pass | Increased | — |
| Storage density | Increased | — |
| SKU size flexibility | — | Reduced (bay volume constrained) |
| Pick-arm dwell time | — | May require faster actuator cycling to avoid bottleneck |
| Deck structural loading | — | More frequent load points increase rack engineering complexity |

The system's throughput ceiling is ultimately set by **whichever is slower**: ATV translational speed between bays, or pick-mechanism actuation time at each bay—meaning pitch reduction yields diminishing returns once actuation time becomes the binding constraint.

---

## 5. Summary

Variable rack pitch functions as a **throughput-tuning parameter** rather than a fixed structural constant. By clustering fast-moving SKUs into tight-pitch zones, the array allows ATVs to convert what would otherwise be many discrete stop-cycle operations into consolidated low-speed passes, extracting multiple picks per aisle traversal while reserving wider pitch for bulkier, lower-frequency inventory where full-speed travel between fewer stops is more efficient.

# Sample Patent Claim Language: Multi-Level Storage Rack System with Shared Rolling Surface

Below is draft claim language for a storage rack system where vehicles traverse multiple levels sharing a common rolling surface, with vertical pitch relationships enabling sequential/ordered retrieval of items.

---

## Independent Claim 1 (System Claim)

**1.** A storage rack system for ordered multi-item retrieval, comprising:

a first storage level defining a first rolling surface configured to support a wheeled vehicle for traversal thereon;

a second storage level disposed vertically above the first storage level, the second storage level defining a second rolling surface configured to support the wheeled vehicle for traversal thereon, wherein the second rolling surface is contiguous with the first rolling surface such that the wheeled vehicle transitions between the first storage level and the second storage level without leaving the common rolling surface;

a plurality of storage positions arranged along each of the first storage level and the second storage level, each storage position configured to hold at least one item;

wherein the first storage level and the second storage level are separated by a vertical pitch distance selected to correspond to a retrieval sequence such that the wheeled vehicle, while traversing the common rolling surface, sequentially accesses storage positions on the first storage level and the second storage level in a predetermined order corresponding to a retrieval manifest.

---

## Independent Claim 2 (Method Claim)

**2.** A method for retrieving a plurality of items from a multi-level storage rack system, comprising:

providing a storage rack system having a first storage level and a second storage level vertically offset from the first storage level by a pitch distance, the first storage level and the second storage level sharing a common rolling surface upon which a wheeled vehicle travels;

receiving a retrieval manifest identifying an ordered sequence of items stored at a plurality of storage positions distributed across the first storage level and the second storage level;

traversing the wheeled vehicle along the common rolling surface between the first storage level and the second storage level, wherein the pitch distance between the first storage level and the second storage level is configured to align the wheeled vehicle with successive storage positions identified in the retrieval manifest without requiring the wheeled vehicle to reverse direction along the common rolling surface; and

retrieving, at each successive storage position, an item corresponding to the ordered sequence identified in the retrieval manifest.

---

## Dependent Claims (Illustrative)

**3.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein the vertical pitch distance is uniform between the first storage level and the second storage level and at least a third storage level, such that the plurality of storage positions are vertically aligned at regular intervals along the common rolling surface.

**4.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein the vertical pitch distance is non-uniform between successive storage levels, and wherein the non-uniform vertical pitch distance corresponds to a variable spacing of the retrieval sequence defined by the retrieval manifest.

**5.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein the common rolling surface comprises a ramped transition portion connecting the first rolling surface of the first storage level to the second rolling surface of the second storage level, the ramped transition portion having a slope configured to permit the wheeled vehicle to ascend or descend between the first storage level and the second storage level while maintaining continuous contact with the common rolling surface.

**6.** The storage rack system of claim 1, further comprising a control system configured to direct the wheeled vehicle along the common rolling surface in accordance with the retrieval manifest, wherein the control system correlates the vertical pitch distance between the first storage level and the second storage level with a horizontal travel distance along the common rolling surface to determine a path of travel for the wheeled vehicle.

**7.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein each of the plurality of storage positions on the first storage level is vertically offset from a corresponding storage position on the second storage level by the vertical pitch distance, such that the wheeled vehicle accesses vertically aligned pairs of storage positions during a single pass along the common rolling surface.

**8.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein the wheeled vehicle comprises a lift mechanism configured to raise or lower an item retrieval component relative to the common rolling surface by an amount corresponding to the vertical pitch distance, thereby enabling the wheeled vehicle to retrieve items from the first storage level and the second storage level without repositioning the wheeled vehicle along the common rolling surface.

**9.** The storage rack system of claim 1, wherein the retrieval sequence corresponding to the vertical pitch distance is determined based on at least one of: an order fulfillment sequence, an item size, an item weight, or an item retrieval frequency.

**10.** The method of claim 2, further comprising adjusting a height of an item retrieval component of the wheeled vehicle by an increment corresponding to the pitch distance between the first storage level and the second storage level, wherein the increment is determined based on the ordered sequence of items identified in the retrieval manifest.

---

## Drafting Notes

- **"Common rolling surface"** language emphasizes structural continuity between levels — critical for distinguishing from prior art with segregated per-level rails.
- **"Vertical pitch distance"** is defined functionally (tied to retrieval sequence) rather than purely structurally, which broadens claim scope while still being definite under § 112(b).
- Consider adding claims directed to the **vehicle itself** (with lift mechanism) as a separate independent claim if the vehicle is a novel component, to obtain a device claim independent of the rack.
- The dependent claims cover **uniform vs. non-uniform pitch**, **ramped vs. steeped transitions**, and **control system logic** — these should be reviewed against your actual embodiments to prioritize which fallback positions matter most for prosecution.

---

**Note:** This is drafting scaffolding based on general patent claim conventions — please have a registered patent attorney or agent review and tailor this to your specific technical disclosure, prior art landscape, and jurisdictional requirements before filing.

# AUTOMATED STORAGE AND RETRIEVAL SYSTEM WITH MULTI-LEVEL DECK ARCHITECTURE AND VARIABLE RACK PITCH FOR OPTIMIZED MULTI-PICK SEQUENCING

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to automated storage and retrieval systems (AS/RS), and more particularly to a multi-level deck architecture in which discrete deck levels define rolling surfaces for autonomous load-handling vehicles, wherein the storage rack structure incorporates variable pitch spacing between storage locations to facilitate efficient sequencing of multi-pick and multi-place operations.

---

## BACKGROUND

Conventional automated storage and retrieval systems typically employ either (a) crane-based shuttle systems operating within fixed-aisle rack structures, or (b) grid-based systems in which autonomous vehicles traverse a two-dimensional surface disposed atop a storage grid, retrieving bins via vertical extension mechanisms. While such systems provide functional density improvements over manual warehousing, they present limitations with respect to (i) vehicle traversal efficiency across multiple storage levels, (ii) throughput degradation during multi-item order fulfillment requiring sequential access to non-adjacent storage locations, and (iii) mechanical complexity associated with vehicles capable of both horizontal and vertical translation.

There exists a need in the art for a storage architecture that decouples vehicle horizontal traversal from vertical bin retrieval mechanics, while simultaneously optimizing the physical arrangement of storage locations to reduce vehicle dwell time and travel distance during multi-pick order fulfillment sequences.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with the present disclosure, an automated storage and retrieval system is provided comprising a multi-level rack structure defining a plurality of vertically stacked deck levels, each deck level comprising a substantially planar rolling surface configured to support the horizontal traversal of one or more autonomous load-handling vehicles thereon. The rack structure disposed beneath, adjacent to, and/or integrated with each deck level defines a plurality of storage locations arranged in rows and columns, wherein the pitch (i.e., center-to-center spacing) between adjacent storage locations along at least one axis is variable rather than uniform.

In certain embodiments, the variable pitch is configured according to a predetermined or dynamically computed spacing schema correlated to (a) statistical retrieval frequency of stored items (e.g., ABC velocity classification), (b) anticipated multi-pick order profiles, and/or (c) vehicle acceleration/deceleration kinematics, such that the physical distance traversed by an autonomous vehicle during execution of a multi-pick sequence is minimized relative to a uniform-pitch baseline configuration.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### 1. General System Architecture

Referring to the exemplary embodiment, the AS/RS comprises a plurality of deck levels **L₁, L₂, ... Lₙ**, each vertically separated by a deck-to-deck spacing sufficient to accommodate the vertical envelope of an autonomous vehicle **(100)**. Each deck level **(200)** comprises:

- A rigid support structure, which may comprise beams, trusses, or a monolithic plate, configured to bear the distributed and point loads of the vehicle(s) and stored inventory;
- A rolling surface **(210)**, disposed on the upper face of the support structure, configured to provide a low-friction, high-traction interface for wheeled or tracked traversal by the autonomous vehicle;
- A plurality of apertures, slots, or channels **(220)** formed in or adjacent to the rolling surface, through which a vehicle-mounted extraction mechanism (e.g., a telescoping shuttle, robotic arm, or vertically actuated gripper) may engage a storage container disposed in a rack position beneath the deck level.

Vertical translation between deck levels is achieved by dedicated lift mechanisms **(300)** — such as vertical conveyors, elevators, or shaft-based hoists — disposed at designated transfer points along the rack structure, obviating the need for individual vehicles to possess independent multi-level climbing capability. This architectural separation of horizontal traversal (vehicle-borne, per-deck) from vertical translation (infrastructure-borne, via lifts) reduces the mechanical complexity, mass, and cost of each autonomous vehicle unit.

### 2. Variable Rack Pitch Configuration

The rack structure underlying or integrated with each deck level defines storage positions **(400₁, 400₂, ... 400ₘ)** arranged along a primary traversal axis. In contrast to conventional uniform-pitch rack designs, the present system defines a pitch function **P(i)**, representing the center-to-center distance between storage position *i* and storage position *i+1*, which varies as a function of position index according to one or more of the following schemas:

**(a) Velocity-Correlated Pitch Zoning:** Storage positions statistically associated with high-frequency SKU turnover (a "fast-pick" zone) are assigned a reduced pitch **P_fast**, clustering high-velocity items into a compact zone reachable with minimal vehicle travel, while lower-velocity ("slow-pick") zones are assigned an increased pitch **P_slow**, where **P_fast < P_slow**.

**(b) Multi-Pick Cluster Optimization:** Pitch spacing is configured such that storage positions statistically co-occurring within common multi-item orders (as determined by historical order-pattern analysis, affinity clustering, or machine-learning-derived co-occurrence matrices) are positioned at reduced pitch intervals relative to one another, notwithstanding their absolute position within the rack, thereby minimizing the cumulative travel distance required for a vehicle to execute sequential picks for a single composite order.

**(c) Kinematic-Efficiency Pitch Grading:** Pitch spacing proximate to deck-level transfer points (e.g., lift interfaces, induction/decant stations) is graded to correspond with the acceleration/deceleration profile of the autonomous vehicle, such that the vehicle achieves cruise velocity across the majority of the traversal path while pitch spacing near terminal points accommodates controlled deceleration without necessitating full-stop/restart cycling at each storage position.

### 3. Multi-Pick Sequencing Logic

A warehouse control system (WCS) or warehouse execution system (WES) **(500)**, operatively coupled to the autonomous vehicle fleet and to an order management system, is configured to:

1. Receive a multi-item order request specifying a plurality of required storage positions;
2. Compute an optimized traversal sequence across the variable-pitch rack structure using a shortest-path or minimum-cost routing algorithm (e.g., a weighted graph traversal wherein edge weights correspond to actual physical pitch distances rather than assumed uniform increments);
3. Dispatch the autonomous vehicle along the computed sequence, such that the vehicle performs sequential extraction operations at each storage position via the deck-level apertures **(220)** without requiring return-to-origin or inter-level transfer between picks, where the multi-pick cluster resides on a common deck level;
4. Where required storage positions span multiple deck levels, coordinate lift mechanism **(300)** scheduling to minimize vehicle wait time at transfer points.

### 4. Illustrative Advantages

The described configuration provides the following technical benefits over conventional uniform-pitch, single-surface AS/RS architectures:

- **Reduced Aggregate Travel Distance:** By spatially clustering co-occurring or high-velocity SKUs via non-uniform pitch, the mean travel distance per multi-pick order is reduced relative to a statistically equivalent uniform-pitch layout.
- **Decoupled Mechanical Design:** Separating rolling-surface horizontal traversal from lift-based vertical translation permits simplified vehicle design, reduced vehicle mass, and improved per-vehicle throughput.
- **Scalable Zoning:** The pitch-variation schema may be dynamically re-computed and, in embodiments employing reconfigurable rack modules, physically adjusted in response to seasonal demand shifts, without requiring wholesale redesign of the deck-level rolling surface.
- **Improved Vehicle Kinematic Efficiency:** Grading pitch near transfer points reduces unnecessary acceleration/deceleration cycling, reducing energy consumption and mechanical wear.

---

## CLAIMS (Exemplary, Non-Limiting)

**1.** An automated storage and retrieval system comprising:
a rack structure defining a plurality of vertically arranged deck levels, each deck level comprising a rolling surface configured for horizontal traversal by at least one autonomous vehicle;
a plurality of storage positions defined by the rack structure and accessible via apertures formed in or adjacent to each rolling surface;
wherein a pitch distance between at least two pairs of adjacent storage positions along a common axis is unequal, such that at least a first pitch distance differs from a second pitch distance.

**2.** The system of claim 1, wherein the pitch distance between storage positions is inversely correlated to a statistically determined retrieval frequency associated with items stored therein.

**3.** The system of claim 1, wherein the pitch distance between a first storage position and a second storage position is reduced relative to a baseline pitch based on a determined co-occurrence frequency of items associated with the first and second storage positions within historical multi-item order data.

**4.** The system of claim 1, further comprising a lift mechanism configured to transfer the autonomous vehicle between deck levels, wherein the autonomous vehicle lacks independent multi-level vertical translation capability.

**5.** The system of claim 1, further comprising a control system configured to compute a multi-pick traversal sequence for the autonomous vehicle based on the variable pitch distances defined by the rack structure.

**6.** The system of claim 1, wherein the pitch distance proximate to a deck-level transfer point is graded according to a predetermined vehicle deceleration profile.

---

*[Additional figures, reference numeral tables, and alternative embodiments — including reconfigurable/adjustable pitch rack modules, multi-axis pitch variation, and hybrid crane/vehicle configurations — may be appended as required for full patent specification compliance.]*

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed technical claim describing a storage system architecture with racks, aisles, and decks arranged so that an autonomous vehicle can perform multiple ordered picks during a single pass through an aisle.
counterfactuals.output:
# Technical Claim: Multi-Level Storage System with Sequential Pick Optimization for Autonomous Vehicles

## 1. Independent Claim

**Claim 1:** A storage and retrieval system comprising:

a) a plurality of storage racks arranged in parallel rows, each storage rack comprising a plurality of vertically-stacked decks, each deck defining a plurality of discrete storage locations configured to hold inventory items or containers;

b) a plurality of aisles, each aisle defined by the space between two adjacent parallel storage rack rows, each aisle providing access to storage locations on both laterally-opposing racks across a plurality of vertical deck levels;

c) at least one autonomous vehicle configured to traverse a given aisle along a longitudinal travel path, the autonomous vehicle comprising:
   (i) a chassis supporting a drive mechanism for bidirectional horizontal movement along the longitudinal travel path of the aisle;
   (ii) a vertically-actuated payload engagement mechanism configured to extend laterally in either of two opposing directions to access storage locations on either adjacent rack, and to raise or lower to align with any of the plurality of deck levels;
   (iii) an onboard control module configured to receive a multi-item pick manifest specifying a plurality of pick tasks, each pick task associated with a distinct storage location defined by an aisle position, a deck level, and a lateral side designation;

d) wherein the control module is configured to:
   (i) determine an execution sequence for the plurality of pick tasks based on the relative aisle positions, deck levels, and lateral sides of the associated storage locations, such that the sequence minimizes redundant longitudinal travel and direction reversals along the aisle;
   (ii) command the autonomous vehicle to execute the plurality of pick tasks according to the determined sequence during a single unidirectional or minimally-reversing pass through the aisle, without requiring the vehicle to exit and re-enter the aisle between individual pick tasks;
   (iii) accumulate a plurality of picked items onboard the autonomous vehicle between successive pick tasks within the same aisle pass, prior to transporting the accumulated items to a designated output location.

## 2. Dependent Claims — Structural Variations

**Claim 2:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the vertically-actuated payload engagement mechanism comprises a telescoping fork, shuttle, or robotic arm capable of independent extension distances calibrated to a rack depth of the storage location, permitting single-deep, double-deep, or multi-deep storage retrieval.

**Claim 3:** The system of Claim 1, wherein each deck further comprises a guide rail, track, or fiducial marker array readable by an onboard sensor of the autonomous vehicle, enabling the control module to verify vertical and lateral alignment with a target storage location prior to executing a pick task.

**Claim 4:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the plurality of decks are spaced at non-uniform vertical intervals corresponding to differing container height classes, and wherein the control module retrieves deck-height metadata from a warehouse management system to compute vertical actuation distances for each pick task in the sequence.

**Claim 5:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the autonomous vehicle further comprises an onboard buffer or carrier structure comprising a plurality of discrete holding cells, each holding cell configured to receive and retain one accumulated item independently of other holding cells, such that items picked at different points along the aisle pass do not physically interfere with one another.

**Claim 6:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the racks comprise a plurality of aisle-facing openings on both lateral faces, and wherein the autonomous vehicle payload engagement mechanism is configured to alternate lateral extension direction between successive pick tasks within the same aisle pass without reversing the vehicle's longitudinal direction of travel.

## 3. Dependent Claims — Sequencing and Control Logic

**Claim 7:** The system of Claim 1, wherein determining the execution sequence comprises applying a traveling-salesman-type optimization heuristic to the set of pick task coordinates, the coordinates comprising an aisle-position value, a deck-level value, and a lateral-side value, to generate a monotonic or near-monotonic ordering along the longitudinal axis of the aisle.

**Claim 8:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the control module is further configured to dynamically re-sequence remaining pick tasks in response to:
   (i) detection of an obstruction at a target storage location;
   (ii) detection of an item discrepancy at a target storage location; or
   (iii) receipt of an updated pick manifest during an in-progress aisle pass.

**Claim 9:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the control module is configured to interleave pick tasks with put-away tasks within the same aisle pass, such that the autonomous vehicle both deposits an item at a first storage location and retrieves an item from a second storage location without exiting the aisle.

**Claim 10:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the multi-item pick manifest is generated by a warehouse management system based on outbound order data, and wherein the control module receives the manifest via a wireless communication interface prior to or during entry into the aisle.

**Claim 11:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the control module computes an estimated aisle transit time for the sequenced pick tasks and transmits the estimated transit time to a fleet management system for coordination with other autonomous vehicles operating in adjacent or intersecting aisles.

## 4. Dependent Claims — Multi-Vehicle and Layout Variations

**Claim 12:** The system of Claim 1, further comprising a plurality of autonomous vehicles operating concurrently within a single aisle at different deck levels, wherein the control modules of the respective vehicles coordinate via a shared communication protocol to avoid vertical or horizontal collision while independently executing sequenced multi-pick tasks.

**Claim 13:** The system of Claim 1, further comprising at least one lift or vertical transport mechanism positioned at an end of the aisle, configured to transfer the autonomous vehicle between the aisle and a different deck-level aisle within the same rack row or an adjacent rack row, such that a single vehicle may execute sequenced pick tasks spanning multiple aisles accessed via the lift.

**Claim 14:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the plurality of storage racks and aisles are arranged in a grid pattern comprising a plurality of parallel aisles intersected by at least one perpendicular cross-aisle, and wherein the autonomous vehicle is configured to transition from a first aisle to a second aisle via the cross-aisle to continue executing the sequenced plurality of pick tasks of a single manifest.

**Claim 15:** The system of Claim 1, wherein the output location comprises a conveyor, pick station, or docking port positioned at an end of the aisle, and wherein the autonomous vehicle is configured to unload the accumulated plurality of picked items at the output location in a single unloading operation following completion of all sequenced pick tasks in the aisle pass.

## 5. Method Claim

**Claim 16:** A method for retrieving a plurality of items from a multi-level storage rack system using an autonomous vehicle, the method comprising:

a) receiving, at an onboard control module, a pick manifest identifying a plurality of storage locations, each storage location defined by an aisle-position coordinate, a deck-level coordinate, and a lateral-side coordinate;

b) computing a sequenced order of the plurality of storage locations to minimize longitudinal travel distance and directional reversals within a single aisle;

c) directing the autonomous vehicle into the aisle and advancing the autonomous vehicle along the longitudinal travel path according to the sequenced order;

d) at each successive storage location in the sequenced order, actuating a payload engagement mechanism to align vertically with the corresponding deck-level coordinate and extend laterally toward the corresponding lateral-side coordinate to retrieve an item;

e) retaining each retrieved item onboard the autonomous vehicle in a discrete holding position until completion of the sequenced order; and

f) transporting the plurality of retrieved items to a common output location following completion of the final pick task in the sequenced order, without the autonomous vehicle having exited the aisle during steps (c) through (e).

**Claim 17:** The method of Claim 16, further comprising dynamically re-computing the sequenced order in response to a real-time change in item availability, obstruction status, or manifest update received during execution of steps (c) through (e).

---

### Notes for Prosecution Strategy
- Independent Claim 1 is drafted broadly (system) to capture the core inventive concept — *single-pass, multi-pick sequencing logic combined with a rack/aisle/deck architecture enabling bidirectional lateral and vertical access*.
- Dependent claims layer in narrower embodiments (buffer cells, TSP-style sequencing, cross-aisle transitions, multi-vehicle coordination) to provide fallback positions.
- Claim 16 mirrors Claim 1 as a method claim to secure parallel protection.
- Consider filing continuation claims directed specifically to the onboard buffer/carrier subsystem and to the dynamic re-sequencing algorithm, as these may constitute separately patentable sub-inventions.
